cards.front: Why does a program need to store data in a file instead of only in variables?
cards.back: Variables **vanish** when a program stops, so a **file** stores data on disk to keep it between runs.
cards.hint: Consider where the data goes once the program has finished running.

cards.front: Why must a program close a file once it has finished writing to it?
cards.back: Closing sends data still waiting in the **buffer** to the disk and releases the file so other programs can open it.
cards.hint: Think about data that has not yet reached the disk.

cards.front: How can a program process every line of a file, even a very long one?
cards.back: Use a **loop** that runs until end of file, reading and processing one line per pass. Only one line is held in memory at a time.
cards.hint: Think about how many lines are in memory at once.

cards.back: A **file mode** is the setting chosen when a file is opened that limits the program to reading, writing or appending.
cards.hint: It is set at the moment the file is opened.

cards.front: A program opens an existing file in write mode to add a new score. What goes wrong?
cards.back: Write mode **erases** the existing content, so the old data is lost. Use append mode when the old data must stay.
cards.hint: Compare what write and append do to existing content.

cards.front: What steps does a program follow to read a text file line by line?
cards.back: Open the file in **read mode**, loop until end of file reading one line per pass, then close the file.
cards.hint: Consider what must happen before the reading starts and after the loop ends.

cards.front: What is the end of file?
cards.back: The **end of file** is the point after the last item of a file, where a further read has no data to return.
cards.hint: It is the point where the lines run out.

cards.front: A program adds a line read from a text file straight to a total. Why is this wrong?
cards.back: The line arrives as a **string**, and adding strings joins them as text. Convert the line to a number before adding.
cards.hint: What type of data does a line from a file arrive as?

cards.front: What happens when a program writes data into a text file?
cards.back: It sends text to the file and adds an **end-of-line marker** after each item. Numbers must be converted to text first.
cards.hint: Think about what starts a new line.

cards.front: What is a buffer in file handling?
cards.back: A **buffer** is a temporary area of memory that holds data on its way to or from a file.
cards.hint: It sits between the program and the disk.

cards.front: Which formula gives the mean of a set of values, given their total and the number of values?
cards.back: $\mathrm{mean}=\frac{\mathrm{total}}{\mathrm{count}}$, where total is the sum of the values and count is how many values there are.
cards.hint: Divide the sum by how many values were added.

cards.front: A file holds the lines 12, 15, 9 and 20, one per line. What are the total and the mean?
cards.back: The total is **56** and the mean is **14**, because $12+15+9+20=56$ and $56 \div 4 = 14$.
cards.hint: Add all four values, then divide by the number of lines.

cards.front: A loop reads lines from a file with no end-of-file test. What error can occur?
cards.back: Reading **past the end of file** has no data to return, causing a **runtime error** that stops the program. Test for end of file before each read.
cards.hint: What happens when there are no lines left to read?
